analysis.one_liner: Raises car fuel-economy standards and cuts taxes for transit use, home efficiency, and renewable power.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees and five subcommittees, never received a hearing or vote, drew no cosponsors, and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have forced cars and light trucks to go significantly farther on a gallon of gas, made federal agencies cut energy waste in their buildings, and let workers pay for bus and vanpool commuting with tax-free dollars. It would have given homeowners tax credits for insulation and solar equipment, paid utilities to help customers save electricity, and created a 10-year tax credit for electricity made from solar, wind, and geothermal power. It also carried something for coal and oil interests: a federal research program for advanced coal technology, a rule that used oil could never be treated as hazardous waste, and a requirement that petroleum importers stock the federal oil reserve.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers, who would save on gasoline as fleet mileage rose from the 27.5 mpg floor toward as much as 35 mpg for cars by 2001 and 40 mpg thereafter. Commuters who take transit or vanpool, who could exclude up to $75 a month of those costs from taxable income. Homeowners who insulate or install renewable energy equipment, low-income households served by the weatherization program, and the renewable power industry, which would get a 2.5-cent-per-kilowatt-hour tax credit for a decade.

how_it_helps.text: Sets binding fuel-economy targets of up to 35 mpg for passenger cars by model years 2001 and after, and up to 40 mpg subject to later modification, with light trucks required to reach up to 30 mpg [S2] [S3].
Lets workers exclude employer-provided transit passes and vanpool commuting worth up to $75 a month from taxable income, reducing the tax advantage that parked in free employer parking [S2] [S3].
Creates a homeowner tax credit covering 15% of insulation and conservation spending and 30% of renewable energy spending up to set caps [S2] [S3].
Creates a 2.5-cent-per-kilowatt-hour tax credit for electricity generated and sold from solar, wind, or geothermal sources, lasting 10 years for capacity built within 6 years of enactment [S2] [S3].

Requires federal agencies to install every energy conservation project in their buildings with a payback under 10 years by 2000, and authorizes weatherization assistance for low-income homes and energy conservation for schools and hospitals through fiscal 1996 [S2] [S3].

Directs state utility regulators to adopt a federal standard removing rate disincentives for utility conservation programs and least-cost supply, so utilities stop profiting only by selling more power [S2] [S3].

Sets energy conservation standards and labeling for lamps, motors, commercial air conditioners, and heating equipment, and requires states to update residential and commercial building energy codes [S2] [S3].
Requires federal fleets to shift to alternative fuels, reaching 50% of passenger vehicles and light trucks by 2000, concentrated in the most polluted areas [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, who would bear the cost of meeting higher mileage standards, and petroleum importers, who would have to finance the Strategic Petroleum Reserve fill at 200,000 barrels a day until it held 1.5 billion barrels. Taxpayers would fund the research programs, federal building retrofits, and tax credits; costs from the fuel-economy rules would partly show up in new-car prices.

drawbacks.text: Higher fuel-economy standards raise compliance costs that automakers would partly pass on in new-car prices, and the bill's formula keyed targets to each manufacturer's own 1988 fleet performance could reward historically inefficient makers relative to efficient ones [S3].

The bill shields used oil from being listed as a hazardous waste under the Solid Waste Disposal Act, easing a compliance burden for the oil and lubricants industry even as it creates a recycling mandate [S2] [S3].

The Strategic Petroleum Reserve fill is financed by a charge on importers, a cost that would flow through to fuel prices, and the bill lets the President draw down the reserve for severe economic problems from price spikes, not just supply interruptions [S3].

The renewable and residential tax credits and research programs are unpaid mandates on the Treasury; the summary authorizes appropriations but the bill text shown specifies only small sums for the used-oil program [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer and efficiency gains — lower gasoline bills, transit tax breaks, cheaper-to-run homes and buildings — are broad and durable, and the main costs fall on concentrated industries. The honest objections are that the fuel-economy formula lets laggard automakers off lightly, the used-oil hazardous-waste exemption is a straight favor to the oil industry bundled into a conservation bill, and the reserve-fill charge lands partly on consumers at the pump. On balance it is a serious efficiency bill with two or three industry riders attached.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with no cosponsors, split across three House committees and five subcommittees, and none of them ever acted on it before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. John Murtha introduced the bill on August 2, 1991; it was referred the same day to the Energy and Commerce, Science Space and Technology, and Ways and Means Committees [S1] [S5].

Over the following six weeks it was divided among five subcommittees — Energy, Environment, Energy and Power, Transportation and Hazardous Materials, and Commerce, Consumer Protection and Competitiveness [S5].
No committee reported the bill, no floor action was ever scheduled, and the congressional record shows no further action after the September 1991 subcommittee referrals [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers avoided the higher mileage standards and petroleum importers avoided paying to fill the Strategic Petroleum Reserve; no one else gained from the bill's death.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a markup or hearing; its Energy and Power and Commerce subcommittees received referrals in September 1991 and took no further action.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the transit-benefit and tax-credit titles in August 1991 and never acted on them.

against.name: House Science, Space and Technology Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill in August 1991 and never acted on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote and drew no cosponsors, so the record shows no partisan pattern — only that a single Democratic sponsor could not move a bill split across three committees.

industries.note: The bill sets binding fuel-economy floors up to 35 mpg for cars and 30 mpg for light trucks by 2001, with a possible 40 mpg thereafter, requiring manufacturers to redesign fleets. Compliance costs would partly reach buyers as higher new-car prices, but drivers would recover them at the pump.

Importers would have to finance the Strategic Petroleum Reserve fill at 200,000 barrels a day up to 1.5 billion barrels, a cost likely passed to fuel buyers. The bill also exempts used oil from hazardous-waste listing, removing a regulatory threat from the lubricants business.

The bill directs a Department of Energy research, development, and demonstration program for advanced coal technologies that cut sulfur and nitrogen oxides, plus a plan for non-fuel uses of coal. It channels federal research dollars toward keeping coal viable under tighter emission limits.

A 2.5-cent-per-kilowatt-hour tax credit for solar, wind, and geothermal power, plus joint-venture commercialization funding, would directly subsidize the young renewables industry. The subsidy comes from the Treasury rather than from consumers' bills.

A federal standard would push state regulators to remove rate structures that penalize utilities for helping customers use less power, and utility conservation subsidies would become tax-free. Utilities would sell less power but gain a regulated business case for efficiency programs.

The bill creates a Bureau of Recyclable Commodities, standardized commodity grades, recyclability labeling, and a mandate that lubricating-oil producers re-refine a rising share of used oil. This builds guaranteed demand for recovered materials.

Manufacturers would face recyclability labeling rules, recall authority, and civil penalties up to $25,000 per day for false recyclability claims. The compliance cost is real but modest next to the fuel-economy obligations on automakers.
